planting.note: Tuck divisions or nursery plugs into crevices of limestone rock or a tufa-style planting pocket with sharp drainage; avoid disturbing the fibrous rhizome mat once established.

directions: This small, drought-adapted fern grips limestone ledges and canyon walls across the Edwards Plateau, its wavy gray-green fronds backed by a dense coat of tan scales that curl and go dormant-looking in extended drought before rehydrating with rain. Site it in a shaded or morning-sun crevice or rock garden pocket with lean, fast-draining alkaline soil rather than regular garden beds, since standing moisture around the rhizome is its main failure point. Once settled it needs no supplemental feeding and tolerates long dry spells far better than most ferns, making it a good companion for columbines and other limestone-ledge natives.

planting.note: Wedge divisions into vertical or overhanging limestone crevices with minimal soil, mimicking the shallow rocky footholds it occupies on canyon bluffs.

directions: Wright's cliffbrake is a wiry, blue-green rock fern that roots directly into thin pockets of soil in limestone cracks and canyon bluff faces across the Edwards Plateau, often growing alongside maidenhair and lip ferns at the base of shaded cliffs. Give it a crevice garden, dry-stacked limestone wall, or steep rocky bed with excellent drainage and dappled shade, since it resents wet feet and heavy clay far more than it minds heat or dryness. Established clumps need essentially no irrigation beyond natural rainfall and slowly form tidy tufted colonies over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring to early summer in the shaded, moisture-retentive leaf litter typical of canyon-bottom woodlands; it spreads quickly by rooting at the nodes.

directions: Horseherb is a low, mat-forming native that carpets the deeply shaded floors of Edwards Plateau canyon woodlands beneath cedar elm, hackberry, and live oak, bearing tiny yellow daisy flowers nearly year-round in mild weather. It thrives in moist, humus-rich shade where turfgrass fails and is increasingly used as a mowable, foot-traffic-tolerant native lawn alternative under trees. Cut back hard or mow occasionally to keep it tidy, and expect it to die back some in hard freezes before resprouting readily from the root crown each spring.

planting.note: Set transplants in spring in a sheltered canyon-slope or rock-garden setting with dappled shade and gritty, well-drained alkaline soil, siting it where winter cold pockets are avoided.

directions: Heartleaf hibiscus is a small, woody-based shrub of the southern Edwards Plateau's rocky canyon slopes and brushy limestone draws, grown for its brick-red, hollyhock-like flowers held above heart-shaped, slightly fuzzy gray-green leaves. It performs best with some afternoon shade and lean, fast-draining soil, and tolerates considerable drought once its taproot is established, though it freezes to the ground in hard winters and regrows from the base. Prune out dead wood in spring and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils that encourage rot at the crown.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring along a shaded canyon-bottom edge or woodland margin in rocky, well-drained limestone soil; allow room for root suckers to form a loose thicket.

directions: Texas prickly ash forms thorny, suckering thickets in the dappled shade of Edwards Plateau canyon bottoms and creek terraces, where its aromatic, citrus-scented foliage serves as a larval host for giant swallowtail butterflies. Grow it in rocky, well-drained alkaline soil along a wildlife hedgerow or woodland edge rather than a tidy border, since it spreads by root sprouts and carries sharp prickles on young stems. It is largely self-sufficient once established, needing only occasional removal of unwanted suckers to control its spread.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring at the base of a trellis, fence, or shrub it can scramble over, in rocky, well-drained limestone soil in dappled canyon shade.

directions: This twining native honeysuckle climbs through understory shrubs and small trees on the shaded limestone slopes and canyon margins of the Edwards Plateau, opening creamy white to pale yellow tubular flowers in spring that draw hummingbirds, followed by red berries favored by songbirds. Give it a support to scramble on and well-drained rocky soil, since it is far more tolerant of drought and limestone than many introduced honeysuckle vines and does not become the aggressive runner that Japanese honeysuckle does. Light pruning after the main spring bloom keeps it shapely without reducing next year's flower show.
